notes: Arctic Systems income tax settlement-provisions test case; Park J dismissed appeal on section 660A arrangement and outright-gift exclusion.

enrichment.short_title: Jones v Arctic Systems: husband-and-wife company dividends and section 660A
key_facts: Mr Jones, an IT consultant, and his wife each owned one share in Arctic Systems Ltd, which earned fees from his personal services.
Mr Jones drew a modest salary while substantial post-tax profits were distributed as dividends, half to Mrs Jones.
HM Revenue contended the structure was a settlement arrangement under section 660A and that Mrs Jones's dividends were Mr Jones's income.
Special Commissioners split 1-1; the presiding commissioner dismissed the appeal by casting vote for 1999/2000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court income tax appeal from Special Commissioners on the settlement provisions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the corporate structure was an arrangement with an element of bounty, section 660A(6) did not apply, and Mrs Jones's dividends were treated as Mr Jones's income.
enrichment.ratio: A husband-and-wife service company paying low salary and high dividends may constitute a settlement arrangement under section 660G where bounty was intended; the outright-gift exclusion in section 660A(6) does not apply where the wife bought her share and the arrangement comprised more than a simple gift.
legal_issues: Whether the Arctic Systems structure was an arrangement within section 660G(1)
Whether Mr Jones was the settlor and Mrs Jones's dividends arose under the settlement
Whether section 660A(6) excluded the case as an outright gift between spouses
Whether the presiding Special Commissioner's casting vote required guidance

Copeman (H.M. Inspector of Taxes) v Coleman (1939) 22 TC 594
Inland Revenue Commissioners v Plummer [1980] AC 896

notes: Court of Appeal race discrimination jurisdiction case; Clarke LJ held tribunals erred in limiting section 8 analysis to the discrimination period.

enrichment.short_title: Saggar v MoD: Race Relations Act jurisdiction for forces member posted abroad
key_facts: Lt Col Saggar, a RAMC consultant anaesthetist of Indian origin, served mainly in Great Britain until posted to Akrotiri, Cyprus in September 1998.
He alleged racial discrimination by his commanding officer between September 1998 and December 1999.
Employment tribunals held he worked wholly outside Great Britain during the alleged discrimination and lacked jurisdiction.
The Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissed his appeal, applying Carver to confine the inquiry to the discrimination period.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on territorial jurisdiction under Part II of the 1976 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the tribunals erred in law by ignoring earlier UK-based employment when deciding whether work was wholly or mainly outside Great Britain; matter remitted.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 8(1) of the Race Relations Act 1976 the relevant period for deciding whether an employee did his work wholly or mainly outside Great Britain is normally the whole employment relationship, not only the period of alleged discrimination.
legal_issues: Construction of section 8(1) employment at an establishment in Great Britain
Whether Carver required disregard of pre-posting UK service
Application of the 1976 Act to armed forces service treated as employment
What period determines wholly or mainly outside Great Britain
linked_authorities: Carver v Saudi Arabian Airlines [1999] ICR 991
Haughton v Olau Line (UK) Ltd [1986] ICR 357
Rhys-Harper v Relaxation Group plc [2003] ICR 867

notes: Commercial Court enforcement of large Nigerian arbitration award; adjournment granted with security under section 103(5).

enrichment.short_title: IPCO v NNPC: enforcement adjournment of Nigerian New York Convention award
key_facts: IPCO obtained a Nigerian arbitration award of about US$152 million against NNPC over delays on the Bonny Export Terminal Project.
David Steel J granted ex parte enforcement; NNPC applied to set aside and to adjourn pending Lagos proceedings to set aside the award.
NNPC argued suspension, public policy based on section 14 of the NNPC Act, and CPR 62.18 formal defects.
The court found NNPC's Nigerian challenge had realistic prospects on duplication, finance charges and force majeure construction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court applications to set aside an ex parte enforcement order, adjourn enforcement, and order security under the Arbitration Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Set-aside application refused except costs for premature enforcement; enforcement adjourned on terms requiring payment of US$13 million indisputably due and US$50 million security in London.
enrichment.ratio: An application to set aside an award in the country of origin does not automatically suspend it under section 103(2)(f); under section 103(5) adjournment with security may balance comity toward Nigerian supervisory proceedings against enforcement prejudice where the challenge is bona fide and neither manifestly valid nor invalid.
legal_issues: Whether the ex parte order should be set aside for CPR 62.18 defects
Whether the award was suspended by Nigerian set-aside proceedings
Whether enforcement offended English public policy via NNPC Act section 14
Appropriate exercise of discretion to adjourn and order security
linked_authorities: Soleh Boneh Ltd v Government of Uganda [1993] 2 Lloyd's Rep 208
Dardana Ltd v Yukos Oil Co [2002] EWCA Civ 543
DST v Rakoil [1987] 2 Lloyd's Rep 246

confidence.notes: Detailed discretion exercise on adjournment and security; set-aside grounds largely rejected.

notes: Leading CFA success-fee guidance from Woolf CJ and Lord Hoffmann; para 11.8(2) held wrong on re-hearing.

enrichment.short_title: Liverpool tripping claim: reasonableness of single-stage CFA success fee
key_facts: A four-year-old child tripped on a grass verge hole; Liverpool City Council admitted liability and the claim settled for £2,500.
The solicitor entered a Law Society model CFA with a single-stage 100% success fee in October 2001.
On detailed assessment the district judge allowed 100% until defence but reduced the fee to 5% thereafter; the circuit judge held no power to vary by period.
The council's second appeal proceeded by re-hearing with Master Hurst as assessor.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal by re-hearing on conditional fee agreement success fee reasonableness and Costs Practice Direction construction.
enrichment.outcome: Declaratory answers: 100% single-stage fee unreasonable; 50% appropriate throughout; no contractual or court power to apply different success fees by period; para 11.8(2) wrong; underlying costs orders undisturbed.
enrichment.ratio: A CFA may contain only one success fee assessed by reference to facts known when it was made; courts cannot use hindsight to reduce recoverable uplift after risks diminish, and Costs Practice Direction para 11.8(2) cannot override the statutory scheme.
legal_issues: Reasonableness of a 100% single-stage success fee at CFA inception
Whether the CFA allowed different fees for detailed assessment
Whether courts may apply differential success fees by period under para 11.8(2)
Proper order where risks reduced after service of defence
linked_authorities: Callery v Gray [2002] UKHL 28
Halloran v Delaney [2003] 1 WLR 28
Atack v Lee [2004] EWCA Civ 1712

confidence.notes: Authoritative declaratory guidance on CFA success fees with structured answers to six issues.

notes: Costs judge reduced post-judgment CFA success fee to 5% in quantum-only brain injury case.

enrichment.short_title: Haines v Sarner: success fee after liability judgment in RTA brain injury claim
key_facts: The claimant suffered severe head injuries in a 2000 road traffic accident and changed solicitors several times.
By October 2003 the defendant admitted 70% liability and judgment was entered; the claim later settled at £425,000.
Anthony Gold Solicitors entered a new CFA on 24 November 2003 with a 60% success fee.
On detailed assessment the paying party argued no real risk remained after the October 2003 win.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Reserved decision on item 82 of a detailed assessment concerning reasonableness of a 60% CFA success fee.
enrichment.outcome: Recoverable success fee assessed at 5%; permission granted to restore the assessment for remaining issues.
enrichment.ratio: Where liability had already been determined before a CFA was entered and the solicitor would recover base costs even if a Part 36 offer were not beaten, only a modest quantum-only success fee is reasonable and well below the level appropriate where base costs remain at risk.
legal_issues: Whether a 60% success fee was reasonable after judgment on liability
Effect of Law Society Conditions defining win and lose
Application of Atack v Lee and Ellerton v Harris to quantum-only cases
What risks justified any success fee after October 2003
linked_authorities: Atack v Lee [2004] EWCA Civ 1712
Callery v Gray [2001] EWCA Civ 1117
Ellerton v Harris (costs decision in Atack litigation)

confidence.notes: Focused costs ruling on one bill item with clear reasoning though limited to post-judgment CFA facts.

notes: Court of Appeal upheld sentence and confiscation but extended time to pay; counterfeit mobile accessory trading.

enrichment.short_title: Sheikh: sentence and confiscation for counterfeit mobile trademark offences
key_facts: Junaid Sheikh pleaded guilty to six counts of unauthorised trademark use in Nadir Traders' wholesale counterfeit mobile phone accessories business.
The business grossed about £3.2 million over two years; family members shared bookkeeping and Far East sourcing roles.
After an unsuccessful attempt to vacate pleas, he was sentenced to 12 months concurrent and a £84,548 confiscation order.
He appealed sentence and confiscation with leave of the single judge.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal against sentence and confiscation order following contested benefit hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on sentence and confiscation; time to pay confiscation and £25,000 costs extended from six and three months to twelve months from sentence.
enrichment.ratio: Serious commercial trademark counterfeiting warrants immediate custody even with strong personal mitigation; confiscation benefit may be assessed using a medium ratio of disputed illicit sales where the civil standard is met, and prison may justify longer time to pay where assets must be realised.
legal_issues: Whether insufficient credit was given for guilty pleas after vacate application
Whether counts were specimen or represented two years' conduct
Whether confiscation benefit assessment was Wednesbury unreasonable
Whether suspension was justified by mitigation including teaching career
linked_authorities: R v Davies [2003] EWCA Crim 3110
R v Ansari [2000] 1 Cr App R (S) 94

confidence.notes: Clear disposition on sentence and confiscation with limited success on payment timing.

notes: Administrative Court dismissed DPP appeal against special reasons finding in excess alcohol case.

enrichment.short_title: DPP v Sharma: special reasons where vodka added to Smirnoff Ice drinks
key_facts: Ratika Sharma drove with 83 microgrammes of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath, about twice the limit.
Magistrates found a friend added 200ml of vodka to two Smirnoff Ice drinks without her knowledge though she knew she drank them.
Expert evidence agreed she would not have exceeded the limit without the added vodka.
Magistrates found no signs of impairment and held special reasons against disqualification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from magistrates' special reasons finding on drink-driving disqualification.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the magistrates' findings were not perverse and special reasons were open on the evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Special reasons may be established where additional alcohol was added without the driver's knowledge, she would not have exceeded the limit without it, and findings on lack of impairment are for the magistrates unless legally perverse; DPP v O'Connor guidance is not a rigid checklist.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates erred in finding unawareness of added alcohol
Whether expert views on expected impairment required rejection of special reasons
Application of DPP v O'Connor and R v Newton principles
Whether carelessness in leaving drinks relevant
linked_authorities: DPP v O'Connor and Chapman [1992] RTR 66
R v David Newton [1974] RTR 451

confidence.notes: Fact-sensitive special reasons review with deference to magistrates' findings.

notes: Court of Appeal upheld service out on confirming bank letter-of-credit claim; Rome Convention Article 4(5) analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Marconi v Panin Bank: jurisdiction and governing law of confirmed letter of credit
key_facts: Marconi supplied telephone equipment to an Indonesian buyer under English-law contracts payable via letters of credit through Standard Chartered Bank London.
Panin Bank confirmed a credit requiring presentation in Jakarta; it rejected drafts for documentary discrepancies after Hastin Bank's insolvency.
Marconi obtained ex parte permission to serve out and pursued about £1.1 million against Panin as confirming bank.
Panin argued Indonesian law governed and England was not the appropriate forum.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal to set aside service out of the jurisdiction and declaration that the court lacked jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; English law governed the beneficiary-confirming bank contract under Rome Convention Article 4(5), and England was the appropriate forum.
enrichment.ratio: For a negotiation credit contemplated to be advised and paid in London, Article 4(5) displaces the Article 4(2) presumption so the confirming bank's contract with the beneficiary is governed by English law; a breach by failing to remit proceeds to London supports service out.
legal_issues: Governing law of confirming bank contract under Rome Convention Article 4
Whether SCB acted as Panin Bank's agent in communicating confirmation
Where the contract was made and breach occurred
Forum conveniens if Indonesian law applied

notes: High Court refused reference on generic Fosamax 70mg abridged authorisation; applied Generics, Novartis and APS.

enrichment.short_title: Merck v MHRA: generic reliance on Fosamax Once Weekly posology data
key_facts: MSD held long-standing authorisations for Fosamax 5mg and 10mg and a 2000 authorisation for Fosamax Once Weekly 70mg with different posology.
Generic companies sought UK authorisation for alendronate 70mg relying on MSD data without further tests.
MSD argued a posology change warranted additional data protection beyond the ECJ trilogy.
The MHRA accepted abridged cross-reference following Generics, Novartis and APS.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review by innovator seeking reference to the Court of Justice on generic abridged marketing authorisation.
enrichment.outcome: Reference refused; Fosamax Once Weekly is a development within Article 10 proviso and generics may cross-refer without further data.
enrichment.ratio: A change in dose schedule generally entails a posology difference implicit in the Article 10 proviso; following Generics, Novartis and APS, a generic identical to product B may rely on data supporting a development of product A authorised for ten years without fresh tests.
legal_issues: Whether posology change falls within Article 10 proviso
Whether multiple differences exclude cross-reference
Effect of MSD's stand-alone rather than hybrid application
Whether Novartis and APS were distinguishable or wrong

Case C-106/01 Novartis Pharmaceuticals UK Ltd v Licensing Authority
Case C-36/03 Approved Prescription Services Ltd v Licensing Authority

notes: QB judgment rejecting employer liability for employee suicide six years after workplace accident.

enrichment.short_title: Corr v IBC Vehicles: employer liability for suicide after workplace head injury
key_facts: Thomas Corr suffered a serious head injury when a metal panel struck him at work in June 1996; liability was admitted.
He developed severe depression and PTSD and attempted suicide before killing himself in May 2002.
His widow claimed under the 1934 and 1976 Acts including loss flowing from the suicide.
General damages for the original injury were agreed at £45,000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial on whether the employer was liable in damages for the deceased's subsequent suicide.
enrichment.outcome: Claim for suicide-related loss rejected; estate recovers agreed general and special damages for the accident injuries only.
enrichment.ratio: An employer's duty to avoid physical injury does not extend to preventing suicide; death by suicide was not a reasonably foreseeable type of damage and Pigney v Pointers, based on Re Polemis, no longer represents good law after The Wagon Mound.
legal_issues: Whether suicide was reasonably foreseeable at the time of the tort
Application of Page v Smith to psychiatric sequelae versus suicide
Whether Hughes v Lord Advocate supports recovery
Availability of novus actus, volenti and contributory negligence defences
linked_authorities: Page v Smith [1996] AC 155
Overseas Tankship (UK) Ltd v Morts Dock & Engineering Co Ltd [1961] AC 388
Reeves v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis [2000] 1 AC 360
